title: HTTP clients: timeouts, retries and deadline budgets
summary: Why java.net.http waits for ever without a timeout, connect versus request timeouts, slow dependencies and bulkheads, which methods and failures may be retried, exponential backoff with jitter and Retry-After, retry amplification across layers, deadline budgets, and testing timeouts without waiting.
lesson:
## No timeout means wait for ever

```java
HttpClient client = HttpClient.newBuilder()
    .connectTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(2))
    .followRedirects(HttpClient.Redirect.NEVER)
    .build();

HttpRequest request = HttpRequest.newBuilder(URI.create("https://prices.internal/v1/sku/42"))
    .timeout(Duration.ofMillis(800))
    .GET()
    .build();

HttpResponse<String> response = client.send(request, HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString());
```

`java.net.http.HttpClient` (JDK 11+) has no request timeout unless you set one: the javadoc says leaving it out is the same as an infinite duration. `connectTimeout` bounds the TCP and TLS setup; `HttpRequest.timeout` makes `send` throw `HttpTimeoutException` (and `sendAsync` complete exceptionally with it) when the response does not arrive in time. Spring's older `RestTemplate` on its default request factory also waits indefinitely. Set both timeouts on every client, deliberately, per dependency.

## A slow dependency is worse than a dead one

A dead service fails fast; a slow one holds a thread, a connection and the user's request for as long as you let it. With 200 request threads and a dependency that answers in 30 s, a burst of traffic parks every thread on it. Short timeouts, a bulkhead (a cap on concurrent calls) and a circuit breaker that stops calling a failing dependency keep one bad service from taking the rest down.

## Retry only what is safe to repeat

GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, PUT and DELETE are idempotent by definition (RFC 9110): doing them twice has the effect of doing them once. A POST is not, unless the server deduplicates it by an idempotency key. A connect timeout is safe to retry for any method, because nothing reached the server; a request timeout is not, because the server may have done the work and only the answer was lost.

## Retry only what may succeed next time

Retry 429 (too many requests), 502, 503, 504 and transport failures. Do not retry 400, 401, 403, 404 or 409: the same request will get the same answer. A plain 500 is usually a bug on the other side, not a blip, so many clients do not retry it either.

## Back off, add jitter, honour Retry-After

Wait before each retry, doubling the wait each time up to a cap, and pick a random point below it ("full jitter") so a thousand clients do not retry in the same millisecond. When the server sends `Retry-After`, use it (capped at what you are willing to wait). Limit attempts, and count them across the whole call chain: three layers that each retry three times turn one failure into 27 calls.

## Budgets: the deadline belongs to the caller

The user's request has one deadline. Each outbound call gets the time that is LEFT, minus a small reserve for building the answer, and never more than its own cap. When too little is left to be useful, fail at once instead of starting a call that cannot finish. Passing the deadline on (a header such as `X-Deadline`) lets the next service stop work nobody is waiting for.

## Test timeouts without waiting for them

Inject a `Clock` and decide timeouts as plain values, then assert on `request.timeout()` and `client.connectTimeout()`: both are readable `Optional`s on the JDK objects. Keep real network tests few, against a local stub server, with timeouts in milliseconds.

quiz.prompt: An `HttpRequest` is built without `.timeout(...)` and sent with `client.send`. The server accepts the connection and never answers. What happens?
choices: send throws HttpTimeoutException after the JDK default of 30 s
send blocks for as long as the server stays silent
send throws at once with HttpTimeoutException
send returns a 504 response it makes up itself
quiz.explanation: Leaving out the request timeout is the same as an infinite one, so send keeps waiting for a response that never comes. There is no hidden 30-second default, the client never invents a 504, and an immediate exception would need a timeout that was set. Set a per-request timeout on every call to a dependency.

choices: Setting up the connection only
The whole call, from connect to the last body byte
Only the TLS handshake, after TCP connects
The time between two chunks of the response body
quiz.explanation: connectTimeout covers establishing the connection; once it is up, how long the response may take is the request's own timeout. It does not bound the whole call or the gaps between body chunks, and it is not limited to the TLS part. Set both, because a connected but slow server is the common case.

quiz.prompt: A POST to create a payment times out after the request was sent. Should the client retry it as is?
choices: Yes, a timeout means the server never saw it
Yes, but only after waiting the full backoff
No, because POST bodies cannot be sent twice
No, not without an idempotency key
quiz.explanation: A request timeout means the answer did not arrive, not that the work did not happen, so a blind retry can charge twice. Waiting longer does not change that, and a body can technically be sent again. With an idempotency key the server returns the first result instead of acting twice, which makes the retry safe.

quiz.prompt: Which failure is safe to retry even for a POST without an idempotency key?
choices: A read timeout after the whole body was sent
A connect timeout: nothing reached the server
A 503 Service Unavailable from the load balancer
A 409 Conflict answer from the payment provider API
quiz.explanation: When the connection never came up, no request reached the server, so repeating it cannot duplicate anything. After a read timeout or a 503 the request did arrive and may have run, and a 409 is a definite answer that a retry will only repeat. Treat transport failures by when they happened, not by their name.

quiz.prompt: Which response is NOT worth retrying?
choices: 429 Too Many Requests
503 Service Unavailable
404 Not Found
504 Gateway Timeout
quiz.explanation: A 404 is a definite answer about the resource, and asking again gets the same answer, so retrying only adds load. 429, 503 and 504 describe a temporary condition on the server or a proxy, which may clear in a moment, ideally after the wait the server suggests in Retry-After.

quiz.prompt: Why add random jitter to exponential backoff?
choices: So that many clients do not retry at the same moment
Because servers reject requests that are evenly spaced
To make the total wait shorter than plain doubling
So that the backoff never reaches its cap
quiz.explanation: Clients that failed together would otherwise retry together, hitting the recovering server with synchronised waves. Jitter spreads them out. Servers do not reject regular spacing, full jitter usually waits less only on average, and the cap still applies. Pick a random delay under the current ceiling.

quiz.prompt: A 429 response carries `Retry-After: 2`. Your backoff would wait 100 ms. What should the client do?
choices: Wait 100 ms: the client controls its own backoff
Retry at once, since 429 means try again
Give up, because 429 is a client error
Wait about 2 seconds, as the server asked
quiz.explanation: Retry-After is the server telling you when capacity will be back, so it overrides your own guess, within a cap you choose. Retrying sooner earns another 429 and adds to the overload, and 429 is precisely the 4xx that is meant to be retried later. Retry-After in seconds is the common form.

quiz.prompt: The gateway retries 3 times, the service behind it retries 3 times, and its database client retries 3 times. One request hits a failing database. How many database calls can that cause?
choices: 3, because only the database client retries it
9, two layers of three
Up to 27, three layers of three
1, since retries are deduplicated
quiz.explanation: Each layer repeats everything beneath it, so three layers of three attempts multiply to 27 calls for one user request. Nothing deduplicates them, and the gateway's retries repeat the service's retries too. Retry in one layer, usually the one closest to the failure, and give the others a budget.

quiz.prompt: A request must finish within 300 ms and 250 ms are already spent. The price call normally gets 800 ms. What timeout should it get?
choices: 800 ms, its usual per-call setting
About 30 ms, the rest minus a reserve, or none
300 ms, the full deadline of the incoming request
No timeout at all, to give the call its best chance
quiz.explanation: Only 50 ms are left, and part of that is needed to build the answer, so the call gets the small remainder, or none at all when that is too little to be useful. 800 ms or 300 ms would outlive the caller, who has already given up, and no timeout means waiting for ever. Budgets flow from the caller's deadline.

quiz.prompt: How can a unit test check that a request is built with an 800 ms timeout without sending it?
choices: Send it to a server that sleeps for 801 ms
Mock HttpClient and capture the arguments of its send call
It cannot: the timeout is private to the request
Assert request.timeout() equals Optional.of(800 ms)
quiz.explanation: HttpRequest exposes its timeout as an Optional, so building the request with an injected clock and asserting on that value tests the decision directly. A sleeping server makes the test slow and timing-dependent, and mocking HttpClient tests the mock. The value is public, so nothing is hidden.

flashcards.back: Leaving it out equals an infinite duration, so a silent server holds the calling thread indefinitely.
One bounds establishing the connection, the other the wait for the response; set both per dependency.

flashcards.front: Which methods may be retried as they are?
flashcards.back: GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, PUT and DELETE; a POST only with an idempotency key the server honours.

flashcards.front: Connect timeout versus read timeout, for retries
flashcards.back: Before connecting nothing reached the server; after sending, the work may already have happened.

flashcards.front: Which statuses are worth a retry?
flashcards.back: 429, 502, 503 and 504; other 4xx answers will repeat, and a plain 500 is usually a bug.
Double the ceiling each attempt up to a cap, and wait a random time under it so clients spread out.
Layers that each retry multiply their attempts; retry in one layer and budget the rest.
Give each call the time left minus a reserve, capped; fail fast when too little remains, and pass the deadline on.

drills.title: Decide whether, and when, to retry a failed call
drills.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "During yesterday's incident our client hammered the payment provider with retries, charged some customers twice, and kept retrying 404s. Write the retry decision."

**Why it matters.** A retry must be SAFE (repeating cannot do the work twice) and USEFUL (the next attempt may get a different answer), and it must fit in the attempts and the time the caller has left. The wait grows exponentially to a cap, with random jitter, unless the server says how long to wait.

**Your task.** Implement `static Decision decide(Call call, Failure failure, int attempt, int maxAttempts, long remainingMs, LongUnaryOperator jitter)`, checking in this order:
1. safe to repeat: a connect timeout (nothing was sent), an idempotent method (`IDEMPOTENT`), or a call with an idempotency key; otherwise `Decision.stop("not idempotent")`
2. worth repeating: a connect or request timeout, or a status in `RETRYABLE`; otherwise `stop("not retryable")`
3. `attempt >= maxAttempts`: `stop("attempts exhausted")`
4. the delay: a `Retry-After` of 1-6 digits means that many seconds, capped at 30,000 ms; any other value is ignored. Without it, `jitter.applyAsLong(ceiling)` with `ceiling = min(100 << (attempt - 1), 5000)` ms
5. a delay that is not shorter than `remainingMs`: `stop("deadline")`; otherwise `Decision.retryAfter(delay)`

**Worked example.** A GET that got 503 on attempt 3, with jitter returning its maximum, waits 400 ms.
hints: Two different questions come first. Could repeating this request do the work twice, and could the next attempt get a different answer?

Decide safety from the failure kind, the method and the idempotency key, then usefulness from the timeout kinds and the retryable statuses, then the attempt count. Only then pick the wait, preferring the server's Retry-After and otherwise a jittered capped doubling, and stop if it does not fit the deadline.

Check safe to repeat, worth repeating and attempts left in that order, parse a short numeric Retry-After into milliseconds with a cap, otherwise jitter a ceiling that doubles from one hundred milliseconds up to five seconds, and stop when the wait is not shorter than the time left.

drills.title: Derive each call's timeout from the caller's deadline
drills.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "The checkout request has a 2-second deadline, yet a price lookup inside it once ran for 30 seconds. Make every outbound call derive its timeout from what is left, and test it without a network."

**Why it matters.** `java.net.http` waits for ever unless you set `connectTimeout` on the client and `timeout` on the request. The useful timeout for one call is the caller's remaining budget minus a small reserve, capped by what that dependency normally needs; when too little is left, failing before sending is better than a call that cannot finish. Both values are readable on the JDK objects, so a test with a fixed `Clock` checks them exactly.

**Your task.** Implement, using the real `java.net.http` builders (nothing is sent):
- `static HttpClient client(Duration connectTimeout)`: that connect timeout, and `HttpClient.Redirect.NEVER`
- `static HttpRequest prepare(URI uri, Instant deadline, Clock clock, Duration perCallCap)`: a GET to `uri` where
  - remaining = from `clock.instant()` to `deadline`; usable = remaining minus `RESERVE` (20 ms)
  - usable below `MIN_USEFUL` (50 ms): throw `DeadlineExceeded("only <remaining ms> ms left")`
  - timeout = the smaller of usable and `perCallCap`
  - header `X-Deadline` = `deadline.toString()`

**Worked example.** 300 ms before the deadline with a cap of 800 ms: the timeout is 280 ms.
hints: The caller has one deadline. Everything this call may spend comes out of what is left of it, and a little must stay behind.

Measure from the clock's instant to the deadline, take off the reserve, refuse when the rest is below the useful minimum, and otherwise use the smaller of that and the cap as the request timeout, with the deadline in a header.

Compute the duration between the clock instant and the deadline, subtract the reserve, throw when it is under fifty milliseconds, choose the smaller of it and the cap, and build a GET with that timeout and the deadline header. Give the client builder the connect timeout and the never-redirect policy.

drills.title: Bug hunt: a retry policy that trusts every timeout
drills.instructions:
**Bug hunt.** The code in the editor is a plausible first attempt at drill 1, "Decide whether, and when, to retry a failed call". It passes some of the tests, but it has one real bug, the kind a reviewer should catch before it ships.

**Your task.** Find the bug and fix it, changing as little as you can; the tests are the same as drill 1's. The spec is unchanged: Implement `static Decision decide(Call call, Failure failure, int attempt, int maxAttempts, long remainingMs, LongUnaryOperator jitter)`, checking in this order:
1. safe to repeat: a connect timeout (nothing was sent), an idempotent method (`IDEMPOTENT`), or a call with an idempotency key; otherwise `Decision.stop("not idempotent")`
2. worth repeating: a connect or request timeout, or a status in `RETRYABLE`; otherwise `stop("not retryable")`
3. `attempt >= maxAttempts`: `stop("attempts exhausted")`
4. the delay: a `Retry-After` of 1-6 digits means that many seconds, capped at 30,000 ms; any other value is ignored. Without it, `jitter.applyAsLong(ceiling)` with `ceiling = min(100 << (attempt - 1), 5000)` ms
5. a delay that is not shorter than `remainingMs`: `stop("deadline")`; otherwise `Decision.retryAfter(delay)`
drills.explanation: The policy treats every timeout as safe to repeat, so a POST whose request was sent and whose answer never came is retried, which is how a payment gets charged twice. Only a connect timeout is safe for any method, because nothing reached the server. The test "a request timeout on a POST is not repeated: the server may have done it" catches it: the policy answers a 100 ms retry instead of "not idempotent". The connect-timeout test still passes, which is why the bug looks like a harmless generalisation. Match the connect timeout exactly, rather than any failure whose kind ends in timeout.
hints: Two kinds of timeout look alike in the code, but only one of them proves that nothing reached the server.
Look at how the safety check decides that a failure may be repeated for any method, and ask which timeout kinds that test lets through.
Let only the connect timeout make a call safe regardless of method, and leave request timeouts to the method and idempotency key rules.
